question: A 12-year-old boy is referred to a pediatric neurologist because of repetitive motions such as blinking or tilting his head. He is brought in by his mother who says that he also clears his throat and hums repeatedly. These actions have been happening for the past year and his mother is concerned. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccinations and is meeting all developmental milestones. On physical exam, he shows no focal neurological deficits and is cognitively normal for his age. He occasionally sharply jerks his head to one side during the physical exam and utters obscene words. Which of the following is most associated with this condition?

options.opb: CAG repeat on the short arm of chromosome 4
options.opd: Severe atrophy of the caudate and putamen
options.ope: X-linked MECP2 mutation with female predominance

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "12-year-old boy with repetitive motions" -> "possible tic disorder" -> "presence of coprolalia" -> "associated with Tourette syndrome" -> "coprolalia is a common symptom" -> 85%

CHAIN: "12-year-old boy with head jerking and throat clearing" -> "symptoms suggestive of Tourette syndrome" -> "Tourette syndrome can include coprolalia" -> "coprolalia is involuntary utterance of obscene words" -> "highly associated with Tourette syndrome" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Repetitive motions and vocalizations in a child" -> "considering tic disorders" -> "coprolalia is a specific symptom" -> "often seen in Tourette syndrome" -> "strong association with the condition" -> 88%

CHAIN: "Physical exam shows no neurological deficits" -> "cognitive function is normal" -> "symptoms align with Tourette syndrome" -> "coprolalia is a hallmark feature" -> "high confidence in association" -> 92%
analysis: The symptoms described in the vignette, including repetitive motions, throat clearing, humming, and the presence of coprolalia (uttering obscene words), are characteristic of Tourette syndrome. Among the options provided, coprolalia is specifically associated with Tourette syndrome, making option 'opc' the most relevant. The other options relate to different conditions: 3 Hz spike-wave patterns are associated with absence seizures, CAG repeats are linked to Huntington's disease, severe atrophy of the caudate and putamen is also associated with Huntington's disease, and MECP2 mutations are related to Rett syndrome, which predominantly affects females. Therefore, the best-supported answer is 'opc'.
